title: From Judgment to Joyful Homecoming
overview: Zephaniah condemns Jerusalem's corrupt leaders and warns of judgment, then ends with a promise that God will gather a humble people and rejoice over them.

parts.label: A city that won't listen (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The woe is aimed at Jerusalem itself: its officials and rulers devour the people like hungry lions and wolves, its prophets cannot be trusted, and its priests defile the temple and twist God's law. God is pictured doing justice faithfully every morning, the usual time courts sat, yet the guilty feel no shame.

parts.label: Warnings ignored (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: God points to nearby nations already ruined, probably including the northern kingdom of Israel, but Jerusalem only grew more eager to do wrong. So God summons the nations for a fiery judgment, rising either as a witness against them or to take prey, since the Hebrew of verse 8 can be read both ways.

parts.label: Nations turned toward God (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: God will make the peoples' speech pure, which likely means those who once prayed to other gods will call on the LORD and serve him together, like people carrying one load on their shoulders. Worshipers come even from beyond the rivers of Cush, far south of Egypt, though scholars debate whether these are scattered Israelites or foreign peoples.

parts.label: A humble few remain (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: God will remove the proud boasters and leave a humble, poor people who rely on him, so Jerusalem no longer carries the shame of its past. Eating and lying down with no one to frighten them is shepherd language for a safe, settled life.

parts.label: A song of joy (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: The mood flips from judgment to celebration: the punishment is lifted and the LORD, called Israel's King, lives among the people. In verse 17 it is God who sings with delight over them, reversing the usual picture of people singing to God.

parts.label: Bringing the scattered home (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: God promises to deal with oppressors, rescue the lame and gather exiles, giving them honor where they were once shamed. Verse 18 is hard to translate and versions differ, but it seems to speak of people grieving because they could not keep their festivals while far from home.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the closing promises were fulfilled in the return from exile in Babylon, are fulfilled in the church made up of all nations, or still point to a future restoration of the Jewish people.
think: What do you think it would feel like to be delighted in, rather than just tolerated, by someone who had seen you at your worst?
